lessons.title: Introduction to JavaScript
objectives: Understand what JavaScript does on the web
lessons.content: JavaScript adds behavior and interactivity to web pages — responding to clicks, updating content, and communicating with servers.
lessons.notes: JavaScript runs in the browser, one line at a time by default.
lessons.mistakes: Confusing JavaScript with Java — they are unrelated languages.
lessons.practice: Log a greeting message to the console.
lessons.challenge: Log your name and the current year in one message.

quiz.question: What does JavaScript add to a web page?

explanation.en: JS responds to clicks, updates content and talks to servers.
explanation.sw: JS hujibu mibofyo, husasisha maudhui na huwasiliana na seva.

hint.en: console.log writes to the developer console.
hint.sw: console.log huandika kwenye console ya msanidi.

explanation.en: console.log outputs values for debugging.
explanation.sw: console.log huonyesha thamani kwa ajili ya kutafuta hitilafu.

quiz.question: Where does JavaScript commonly run?
options: In the browser (and on servers with Node.js)

hint.en: Every browser has an engine for it.

explanation.en: Browsers run JS; Node.js runs it on servers.
explanation.sw: Browser huendesha JS; Node.js huiendesha kwenye seva.

lessons.title: Variables
objectives: Declare variables with let and const
lessons.content: Variables store values. Use const for values that won't be reassigned, and let for values that will change over time. Avoid var in modern code.
lessons.notes: const doesn't mean immutable — it means the binding can't be reassigned.
lessons.mistakes: Reassigning a const, which throws an error.
lessons.practice: Declare a const for your name and a let for a counter that changes.
lessons.challenge: Try reassigning a const and observe the error in the console.

quiz.question: Which keyword declares a value that will NOT be reassigned?

explanation.en: Use const by default and let only when the value changes.
explanation.sw: Tumia const kwa kawaida na let pale thamani inapobadilika.

explanation.en: let allows reassignment, so the value becomes 1.
explanation.sw: let inaruhusu kubadilisha, kwa hiyo thamani inakuwa 1.

explanation.en: Reassigning a const throws an error.
explanation.sw: Kubadilisha const husababisha hitilafu.

lessons.title: Data Types
objectives: Use typeof to inspect a value
lessons.content: JavaScript has several primitive types: string, number, boolean, undefined, and null, plus objects and arrays as structured types.
lessons.notes: typeof null returns "object" — a well-known historical quirk of the language.
lessons.mistakes: Confusing null (intentional empty value) with undefined (not yet assigned).
lessons.practice: Create one variable for each primitive type and log their typeof.
lessons.challenge: Log the typeof an array and explain what you observe.

hint.en: JS has one numeric type for ints and decimals.
hint.sw: JS ina aina moja ya namba.

explanation.en: All numbers are of type number.
explanation.sw: Namba zote ni za aina number.

explanation.en: Booleans are the unquoted values true and false.
explanation.sw: Boolean ni true na false bila nukuu.

explanation.en: Text values are strings.
explanation.sw: Maandishi ni string.

lessons.title: Operators
lessons.content: Operators perform calculations (+, -, *, /) and comparisons (===, !==, <, >). Always prefer strict equality (===) to avoid type coercion surprises.
lessons.notes: == coerces types before comparing; === does not.
lessons.mistakes: Using == when you mean === leads to subtle bugs.
lessons.practice: Compare two values with both == and === and note the difference.
lessons.challenge: Write an expression that uses at least three different operators.

explanation.en: Strict equality does not convert types.
explanation.sw: Strict equality haibadilishi aina.

explanation.en: Loose equality coerces the string to a number.
explanation.sw: Loose equality hubadilisha string kuwa namba.

explanation.en: Strict comparison gives fewer bugs.
explanation.sw: Ulinganisho mkali hupunguza makosa.

lessons.title: Strings
lessons.content: Template literals (backticks) allow embedding expressions directly in strings using ${}. Strings also have built-in methods like toUpperCase() and slice().
lessons.notes: Template literals make multi-line strings and interpolation far cleaner.
lessons.mistakes: Concatenating with + everywhere instead of using template literals.
lessons.practice: Build a greeting string using a template literal and a variable.
lessons.challenge: Use .toUpperCase() and .length on a string of your choice.

explanation.en: Only backticks evaluate ${} expressions.
explanation.sw: Backtick pekee hutathmini ${}.

explanation.en: toUpperCase returns a new uppercase string.
explanation.sw: toUpperCase hurudisha string mpya ya herufi kubwa.

explanation.en: slice(start, end) excludes the end index.
explanation.sw: slice(start,end) haijumuishi index ya mwisho.

lessons.title: Numbers
lessons.content: JavaScript has a single number type for both integers and decimals. The built-in Math object provides helpers like Math.round() and Math.random().
lessons.notes: Floating point math can produce tiny rounding errors — this is normal.
lessons.practice: Round a decimal number using Math.round().
lessons.challenge: Generate a random integer between 1 and 10.

quiz.question: How many number types does JS have for ints and decimals?

explanation.en: JS uses one number type for both.
explanation.sw: JS hutumia aina moja ya namba.

hint.en: random is 0 to <1; floor gives 0–9; then +1.

explanation.en: The result is a whole number from 1 to 10.
explanation.sw: Matokeo ni namba kamili kutoka 1 hadi 10.

explanation.en: Math.round rounds to the nearest integer.
explanation.sw: Math.round huzungusha hadi namba kamili iliyo karibu.

lessons.title: Arrays
lessons.content: Arrays store ordered lists of values. Items are accessed by index, and methods like push() and pop() add or remove items from the end.
lessons.notes: Arrays are zero-indexed — the first item is at index 0.
lessons.mistakes: Assuming array length changes automatically reflect in old references incorrectly.
lessons.practice: Create an array of three languages and log the second item.
lessons.challenge: Push a new language onto the array and log the updated array.

explanation.en: The array now has 4 items.
explanation.sw: Array sasa ina vipengele 4.

quiz.question: Which index is the FIRST item?

explanation.en: Arrays are zero-indexed.
explanation.sw: Array huanza index 0.

explanation.en: pop removes and returns the last element.
explanation.sw: pop huondoa na kurudisha kipengele cha mwisho.

lessons.title: Objects
lessons.content: Objects group related data using key-value pairs. Properties are accessed with dot notation or bracket notation.
lessons.notes: Bracket notation is required when the key is dynamic or not a valid identifier.
lessons.mistakes: Forgetting quotes around string keys that contain spaces.
lessons.practice: Create a learner object with name, level and goal properties.
lessons.challenge: Add a new property to the object after creating it.

quiz.question: How do you read the goal property?

explanation.en: Use object.property or object['property'].
explanation.sw: Tumia object.property au object['property'].

explanation.en: Each property has a key and a value.
explanation.sw: Kila property ina key na value.

explanation.en: Bracket notation allows dynamic keys.
explanation.sw: Bracket notation huruhusu key zinazobadilika.

lessons.title: Conditions
lessons.content: Conditional statements let your program make decisions using if, else if, and else, combined with logical operators like && and ||.
lessons.notes: Truthy and falsy values matter — 0, "", null and undefined are all falsy.
lessons.mistakes: Forgetting an else branch when one is actually needed.
lessons.practice: Write an if/else that checks if a number is even or odd.
lessons.challenge: Add an else if branch for a third condition.

quiz.question: What does this print?

explanation.en: The first true branch runs.
explanation.sw: Tawi la kwanza lenye kweli hutekelezwa.

explanation.en: && is true only if both sides are true.
explanation.sw: && ni kweli tu kama pande zote mbili ni kweli.

explanation.en: || is true if at least one side is true.
explanation.sw: || ni kweli kama upande mmoja angalau ni kweli.

lessons.title: Loops
lessons.content: Loops repeat code. A for loop is ideal when you know how many times to repeat; array methods like forEach() iterate directly over items.
lessons.notes: Watch for off-by-one errors in loop conditions.
lessons.mistakes: Creating an infinite loop by forgetting to update the loop variable.
lessons.practice: Use a for loop to log numbers 1 through 5.
lessons.challenge: Use forEach to log every item in an array of your choice.

quiz.question: How many times does this loop run?

explanation.en: The condition i<=5 includes 5.
explanation.sw: Sharti i<=5 linajumuisha 5.

explanation.en: ++ increments by one.
explanation.sw: ++ huongeza kwa moja.

quiz.question: Which method iterates directly over array items?

explanation.en: forEach runs a function for every item.
explanation.sw: forEach hutekeleza function kwa kila kipengele.

lessons.title: map, filter & reduce
lessons.content: map() transforms every item into a new array, filter() keeps only matching items, and reduce() combines all items into a single value.
lessons.notes: These methods return new arrays and don't mutate the original.
lessons.mistakes: Forgetting to return a value inside the map/filter callback.
lessons.practice: Use map() to double every number in an array.
lessons.challenge: Chain filter() and map() together in a single expression.

quiz.question: What does map() return?
options: A new array with each item transformed

explanation.en: map returns an array of the same length.
explanation.sw: map hurudisha array yenye urefu ule ule.

explanation.en: filter keeps items where the test is true.
explanation.sw: filter huweka vipengele ambavyo jaribio ni kweli.

explanation.en: reduce combines all items into one result.
explanation.sw: reduce huunganisha vipengele vyote kuwa matokeo moja.

lessons.title: Functions & Scope
objectives: Understand function declarations vs arrow functions
lessons.content: Arrow functions offer concise syntax and don't bind their own 'this'. Variables declared with let/const are block-scoped, unlike var.
lessons.notes: Arrow functions are a great default for callbacks where you don't need 'this' rebinding.
lessons.mistakes: Using an arrow function as an object method when you need 'this' to refer to the object.
lessons.practice: Rewrite a function declaration as an arrow function.
lessons.challenge: Demonstrate block scope with a let variable inside an if block.
lessons.code:
const add = (a, b) => a + b;
console.log(add(2, 3));

quiz.question: What is a key feature of arrow functions regarding this?
options: They do not bind their own this
They always bind a new this

explanation.en: Arrow functions use the surrounding this.
explanation.sw: Arrow functions hutumia this ya mazingira.

quiz.question: What does this print?
quiz.code:
const add = (a, b) => a + b;
console.log(add(2, 3));

explanation.en: Single expression arrows return automatically.
explanation.sw: Arrow ya usemi mmoja hurudisha kiotomatiki.

explanation.en: Unlike var, they live inside the block.
explanation.sw: Tofauti na var, huishi ndani ya block.

lessons.title: Promises & Fetch
lessons.content: Promises represent a value that will be available later. async/await lets you write asynchronous code that reads like synchronous code.
lessons.notes: Always wrap await calls in try/catch to handle network errors gracefully.
lessons.mistakes: Forgetting to await a promise, resulting in a pending Promise object instead of data.
lessons.practice: Write an async function that logs 'done' after a simulated delay.
lessons.challenge: Add a try/catch block around your async logic.

quiz.question: What is a Promise?
options: A value that will be available later

explanation.en: Promises represent eventual completion of async work.
explanation.sw: Promise huwakilisha kukamilika kwa kazi ya async baadaye.

quiz.question: What does await do inside an async function?

explanation.en: await unwraps the resolved value.
explanation.sw: await hutoa thamani iliyotatuliwa.

quiz.question: How do you handle errors with async/await?

hint.en: As shown in the lesson code.

explanation.en: Wrap awaited calls in try/catch.
explanation.sw: Funika miito ya await kwa try/catch.

lessons.title: DOM Manipulation
lessons.content: The DOM (Document Object Model) represents the page as a tree JavaScript can read and modify. querySelector finds elements, and addEventListener responds to interaction.
lessons.notes: Event delegation (listening on a parent) scales better than binding listeners to every child.
lessons.mistakes: Querying the DOM repeatedly inside a loop instead of caching a reference.
lessons.practice: Select a button and change its text when clicked.
lessons.challenge: Add a class to an element on click instead of inline styling it directly.

explanation.en: It returns the first matching element.
explanation.sw: Hurudisha kipengele cha kwanza kinacholingana.

quiz.question: Which method reacts to a click?

explanation.en: addEventListener registers a handler.
explanation.sw: addEventListener husajili kidhibiti.

explanation.en: It updates the element's text.
explanation.sw: Hubadilisha maandishi ya kipengele.

lessons.title: Closures Deep Dive
objectives: Use closures to create private state
lessons.content: A closure is a function that remembers the variables from where it was defined, even after that outer function has finished running — enabling private state without classes.
lessons.notes: Closures are the mechanism behind patterns like counters, memoization and module encapsulation.
lessons.mistakes: Accidentally sharing a closed-over variable across loop iterations with var instead of let.
lessons.practice: Write a counter function that returns increment and getValue functions sharing private state.
lessons.challenge: Explain, in your own words, why the counter's variable can't be accessed directly from outside.

quiz.question: What is a closure?
options: A function that remembers variables from where it was defined

explanation.en: The inner function keeps access to outer variables.
explanation.sw: Function ya ndani huendelea kufikia variables za nje.

quiz.question: What does counter.value() return after one counter.inc()?

explanation.en: inc raised count to 1, value reads it.
explanation.sw: inc iliongeza count hadi 1, value huisoma.

hint.en: count cannot be touched from outside.

explanation.en: Hidden variables are exposed only via the API.
explanation.sw: Variables zilizofichwa hufikiwa kupitia API pekee.

lessons.title: Performance Patterns
lessons.content: Debouncing limits how often a function runs in response to fast events like scrolling or typing. Event delegation attaches one listener to a parent instead of many to children.
lessons.notes: Event delegation is a key technique for large, dynamically rendered UIs.
lessons.mistakes: Attaching a listener to every list item instead of delegating to the parent.
lessons.practice: Write a debounce function that delays execution by 300ms.
lessons.challenge: Apply event delegation to a list with dynamically added items.

quiz.question: What does debouncing do?
options: Limits how often a function runs during rapid events

hint.en: Think of typing in a search box.

explanation.en: It waits until events pause before running.
explanation.sw: Husubiri matukio yakome kabla ya kutekeleza.

quiz.question: Why use event delegation?
options: One listener on a parent instead of many on children

explanation.en: Events bubble up to the parent.
explanation.sw: Matukio hupanda hadi kwa mzazi.

quiz.question: In debounce, what does clearTimeout(timer) do?

explanation.en: Each new event cancels the previous timer.
explanation.sw: Kila tukio jipya hufuta timer ya awali.

lessons.title: Design Patterns in JS
lessons.content: The module pattern uses closures to expose a small public API while hiding internal details — the same idea behind this Academy's own wtca* namespace. The observer pattern lets objects subscribe to events without tight coupling.
lessons.notes: Modern ES modules provide native scoping, but the underlying closure-based pattern still appears everywhere.
lessons.mistakes: Tightly coupling unrelated parts of an app instead of communicating through events.
lessons.practice: Sketch a simple pub/sub object with subscribe() and publish() methods.
lessons.challenge: Implement publish() so it calls every subscribed callback with a payload.

quiz.question: The module pattern uses what to hide internals?

explanation.en: Closures keep private state.
explanation.sw: Closures hudumisha hali ya faragha.

quiz.question: What does the observer (pub/sub) pattern allow?
options: Objects to subscribe to events and be notified

explanation.en: Publishers notify all subscribed handlers.
explanation.sw: Wachapishaji huarifu vidhibiti vyote vilivyojisajili.

quiz.question: In the bus example, what does publish(data) do?
options: Calls every subscribed handler with data

explanation.en: Each handler receives the data.
explanation.sw: Kila handler hupokea data.
